title: Post-Course Portfolio: Authentication & User Management System
descriptionMarkdown:
# Authentication & User Management System

## Position in the curriculum
Post-course portfolio expansion: build after finishing the full curriculum through the final capstone. This project is a prerequisite building block for several later catalog entries (Online Quiz Platform, Forum/Reddit-Style Backend, E-commerce Backend, Project Management App, Food Delivery Backend) that all need real authentication rather than an assumed caller identity — build or at least design this one first.

## Beyond what the lessons taught
Spring Security and JWT are not covered by the 25-chapter curriculum, which teaches the underlying concepts (authentication versus authorization, password hashing, secrets handling, object-level authorization) without a specific security framework. Treat learning Spring Security's filter chain and a JWT library as required, deliberate self-directed research for this project, using the official Spring Security reference documentation as your primary source.

## Already-proven foundation
Chapter 23 already required you to explain why a fast general-purpose hash is unsuitable for password storage and to design object-level authorization checks. This project is where those two concepts stop being reasoned about in the abstract and become a real, runnable login flow.

## Project scope
A `User` entity with a bcrypt- or Argon2-hashed password (never a fast digest), a `POST /api/auth/register` endpoint (rejecting a duplicate email with a real database `UNIQUE` constraint, not just an application check), and a `POST /api/auth/login` endpoint issuing a signed JWT on success. Protect at least two resources behind the token: one requiring only authentication (any logged-in user), and one requiring a specific role (an `ADMIN`-only endpoint, using role-based authorization). Add one object-level authorization check on a per-resource endpoint (a user may only view or edit their own profile, verified against the authenticated identity, never merely against a client-supplied ID). Implement token expiry and a documented, tested refresh or re-login flow.

## Required evidence
- A password-hashing test confirming two hashes of the same password differ (due to salting) and both still verify.
- An authorization test matrix: unauthenticated request rejected, authenticated-but-wrong-role request rejected, authenticated-and-correct-role request accepted, and a request for another user's own-resource data rejected even though the caller is authenticated.
- A test confirming an expired token is rejected, not silently accepted.
- Evidence that no password, hash, or token ever appears in application logs, using the redaction discipline from Chapter 23.
- A threat-model note (assets, actors, entry points) for this specific service, per Chapter 23's Lesson 1.

## Review and completion
A reviewer registers two accounts, logs in as one, and attempts to read or modify the other account's protected resource using a syntactically valid but unauthorized token — this must fail with the correct status, not a stack trace, and the object-level check (not merely the presence of a valid token) must be what stops it.
learningObjectives: Store passwords with a dedicated slow, salted hashing algorithm and prove it with a test, never a fast digest
Issue, validate, and expire JWTs correctly, including a tested rejection of an expired token
Distinguish authentication failure, role-based authorization failure, and object-level authorization failure as three separate, separately-tested outcomes
Keep secrets, hashes, and tokens out of logs using the same redaction discipline as the security chapter
Research and apply a real security framework (Spring Security) beyond what the lessons taught, using its official documentation
